content_excerpt: A free coding agent that runs entirely on your device, AI model included. Your prompts and code never leave it. Larger models take longer to download and use more of your device. Smaller ones are quicker but less reliable at tool calls. Start downloads the model unless it is already saved in your browser. On weaker devices the browser may stop responding for a while. Open-weight models, licensed under Apache 2.0 , downloaded from Hugging Face the first time you choose one. They're saved in your browser's storage, so later visits don't download them again. A fork of Little Coder , which adapts the Pi agent harness for smaller models. PiPod's changes improve the harness and its compatibility with BrowserPod. Models run on your device's GPU through WebGPU , using LiteRT-LM , whose runtime is compiled to WebAssembly . The legacy engine, Sipp , runs llama.cpp compiled to WebAssembly, also on WebGPU. title: AI coding agent lacks context
content_excerpt: You have 1 article left to read this month before you need to register a free LeadDev.com account. Generating code is now cheap. Getting it to fit a 15-year-old codebase is where the hours go. That’s the argument in The AI Coding Drift Report from DesignVerse. The company studied 15 private enterprise codebases across aviation, banking, and defense. Each was between 15 and 20 years old and held more than one million lines of code. If you’ve worked in a system like that, you know the code that matters most is often the least documented . In one case, the research estimated that a year’s work on a single product would require 9,600 engineering hours without what DesignVerse calls an enterprise context layer. The layer gives AI tools access to the organization’s existing code, architecture, and technical standards. With it, the total fell to 4,000 hours, a 58% reduction. DesignVerse values the 5,600 hours saved at around $882,000, or about three engineers’ worth of capacity. The company presents that as time that could go to other work and doesn’t claim a cut in staffing costs. That framing will go down better in a planning meeting. The more telling figure is what the agents built. DesignVerse compared two unmanaged AI coding agents with its own context-engineered system. The context-engineered system used the organization’s own internal components 92% of the time. The unmanaged agents managed 55% to 59%, and the rest of the time they invented components or swapped in public alternatives. Anyone who has reviewed a pull request that quietly reimplements a helper the team wrote a decade ago will recognize the pattern . Consistency followed the same shape. With context, 97% of repeated runs gave the same answer. Without it, the figure was 61% to 69%. “If companies are paying for AI to write code, only to pay their engineers to fix it afterwards, they need to ask some serious questions about the return on that investment,” says Andrei Manolache, CEO and cofounder of DesignVerse. Most teams can’t see this cost yet. In LeadDev’s AI Impact Report 2026, 31% of respondents said their organization measures AI’s impact, and 68% named a lack of clear metrics as a challenge. Token usage was the most common metric among organizations that measure AI’s impact, with 58% tracking it. The same share of respondents rated token metrics ineffective. title: Announcing vLLM-GR: Efficient Inference for Generative Recommendation
summary: vLLM-GR extends vLLM to serve generative recommendation models with accelerator-side beam search, catalog constraints, and shared KV caching across candidate paths.
story_key: model:vllm|title:announcing vllm gr efficient inference for generative recommendation
content_excerpt: Today we’re introducing vLLM-GR , an open-source inference and serving framework built on vLLM for generative recommendation models. Consider a video feed. Given a viewer’s history, a model such as OneRec can generate a semantic ID (SID) for a video the viewer might watch next. To assemble a feed, the application needs a set of candidates. vLLM-GR extends vLLM’s model execution and paged key-value (KV) cache with beam search that explores multiple candidate IDs in one request. The overview shows how recommendation models generate item IDs or score supplied candidates. The OneRec-1.7B example below follows the generation path, from a viewer’s history to 128 candidate SIDs. A recommendation service has to turn a long interaction history into a set of candidates within a single request’s latency budget. Generating each item ID may take only a few tokens, yet the engine must explore many paths and return items the application can serve. vLLM-GR builds its recommendation search into the vLLM engine. vLLM supplies the scheduler, model execution, and paged KV cache. vLLM-GR adds a beam session that spans the whole search and keeps track of how candidate paths branch. EngineCore owns each beam session from admission to completion. The scheduler dispatches prefill and decode stages to a worker. At each stage, the model runner scores the next token and beam selection records the score and parent of each surviving path. The next decode uses those parent indices to read the right KV state. One request returns two candidates with beam widths of 2 → 3 → 2. The catalog filters out A1 · B1 because no item starts with that prefix. A full-vocabulary search skips this filter. The SIDs and scores are illustrative. In the prefill–decode–decode (PDD) pipeline, the scheduler admits a BeamSearch() request and dispatches its prefill stage to the worker. Prefill scores the first SID component while the host prepares decode 1. During decode 1, the host prepares decode 2. The second decode inherits the selected parents’ suffix KV and completes two SIDs. Green marks the component selected at each stage. The benchmarks measure P99 latency to show how beam width and batch size affect tail latency for generative recommendation. The two overview charts hold the input length at 1,024 tokens and compare beam widths of 256 and 128 at batch sizes 1, 4, and 8 across four NVIDIA GPUs and two Ascend NPUs. title: DKnown-Jev-2: Article-Level Answer-Evidence Classification and Efficient Inference with a Pre-trained Language Model
summary: Evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering requires determining whether a candidate article contains content that directly supports an answer under the applicable conditions of the question. We present DKnown-Jev-2, an article-level answer evidence classifier designed for evidence integration across multiple paragraphs. The model jointly encodes question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, and uses a pointer-style classification head to predict Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE) in a single forward pass. Ona manually annotated test set of 972 evaluation instances, DKnown-Jev-2 achieves 91.77% accuracy and 91.28% macro-F1, outperforming Jev by 2.16 and 2.37 percentage points, respectively, while reducing both evidence misses and non-evidence false positives. The test set contains 317 multi-paragraph instances, with a maximum body length of 9,322 characters. Shared article encoding and non-autoregressive classification support low-latency inference. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for article-level evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering.

title: mini-psych-agent: Evaluating Human-Like Behavior in LLM Agents through Interactive Psychological Environments
summary: A Large Language Model (LLM), its harness, and the test-time compute budget jointly determine its behavior. Consequently, the same underlying model, embedded in different agentic workflows or allocated different amounts of test-time compute, can exhibit markedly different performance. Psychologists face an analogous challenge when evaluating human performance: the same person may behave differently under different incentives and levels of deliberation. Psychological tasks therefore provide an ideal testbed for studying such behavioral variation. However, when adapted to LLMs, these tasks are typically text-transcribed, replaying fixed, language-rendered experiments as static prompts. This format is ill-suited to agent evaluation, where actions can alter future observations and task states. Conversely, although dynamic environments are prevalent in the evaluation of LLM agents, they rarely ask whether the resulting behavior is human-like. Here, we bridge this gap by transforming psychological tasks into dynamic environments in which agents can interact and by using a learned human-policy model to evaluate how compatible the resulting behavioral trajectories are with human behavior. Across these environments, we find that this compatibility varies with an LLM's agentic configuration and the psychological task, and that memory raises it mainly by making choices more predictable rather than more human-like. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation of LLM agents in psychology-inspired environments, accounting for both the backbone model and its agentic scaffold.

title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
summary: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
story_key: model:vllm|variant:mini|title:inkling 2 mini on vllm day 0 support for a looped model
content_excerpt: Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research , on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini . You can serve the model with: And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before. Prelude, core, coda. The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the block attention residuals used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. Every pass starts from the prelude's output. A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. Messages are read at every sublayer. From the second pass on, each core sublayer input (the attention's query, key and value inputs and the MLP input) gets its own message, read from the previous pass's two blocks by an attention-residual read with a learned query per layer and input type. A rank-64 controller then merges the message into the input, per channel: With 12 core layers and 4 inputs each, every later pass reads 48 messages per token. Because the query, key and value inputs get different messages, the sliding-window layers, which project all three from one input in the first pass, take three separate inputs in later passes. Each pass keeps its own memory. Every core layer has a KV cache and a conv-state cache per pass, so pass p attends to the keys and values that pass p computed for earlier tokens. The model has 24 layers but 48 KV caches and 48 conv-state caches. DSpark draft from inside the loop. title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
summary: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

title: SayDo: Benchmarking the Safety of Frontier Models from Chat to Closed-Loop Robot Control
summary: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.

title: vllm v0.34.0
summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 In most cases it's now best to not set gpu_memory_utilization. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542
Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed — #64287

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR
Mistral Large 4 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. #64534
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

Performance

Improvement Hardware Gain PR
Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen 4×GB200 up to 1.95× decode #65152
GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE NVIDIA 1.6× output throughput vs DEP4 #60895
Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) GB300 1.5× single-stream decode #64077
Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) GB200 GLM-5.3 TTFT 1.24–1.40× faster at 32K–128K #63956
KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) GB300 1.34–1.59× decode attention #63638
Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) NVIDIA 3.0–8.8% lower decode ITL #51012
FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark 8×MI355X +35–57% interactivity at conc. 1–8 #63440

AMD ROCm

  • Release images and wheels are ROCm 10.0 only (#61939).
  • MoRI EPv2 via --all2all-backend mori (#61361).
  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

Install

Python wheels

Platform Install
CUDA 13.0 (PyPI) pip install vllm
CUDA 13.0 (uv) uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto
ROCm 10.0 pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100
XPU uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match

Docker images

Platform Image Short alias
CUDA 13.0 (default) vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0
CUDA 13.0 + DeepEP over AWS EFA vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0-efa vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-efa
ROCm 10.0 vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-rocm
CPU vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-cpu
XPU vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:v0.34.0 vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-xpu

latest tags work the same way (e.g. vllm/vllm:latest-rocm). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The -efa image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576).

The Assets section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels.

Full changelog

Model support
  • Mistral Large 4 (#64534) runs on MRV2 with:
    • sparse MLA plus the DSA indexer, and cross-layer KV sharing;
    • DSpark, DCP/PCP, NIXL P/D and HiSparse.
  • Other new models:
    • MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (#64111), plus P/D across different prefill and decode TP (#64475).
    • Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe with MTP and DFlash2 (#64282, #64944).
  • DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1
    • Prefill gathers compressed KV once per KV-source group: 38 → 4 gathers per step (#59131).
    • Decoder replay graphs share the model graph pool: prefill graph memory 15.52 → 9.88 GiB per rank on GB200 (#63155).
    • fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant 3.5× faster, prefill 6% faster (#63540).
    • DSpark/MTP memory savings of about 512 MiB per GPU (#63996).
    • Engram host tables shared across DP ranks (#62359).
    • DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits on the FP8 indexer cache (#62011).
    • Packed multi-image vision encoding, 1.6–2.6× (#65030).
    • LoRA on the language model, compressor and wo_a layers (#57245, #64880).
    • DSpark with PCP (#61994); PCP with PP or DP (#63098).
    • Fixes: sparse prefill in FULL CUDA graphs (#59986), prefill memory budgeting (#63047), MTP embedding under PP (#65816), DeepSeek-V3.2 PP (#59961).
  • GLM
    • GLM-5.3-Flash: DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE (#60895), adaptive verification (#60229), row-strided QKV into FlashKDA (#61614).
    • GLM-5.3 FP8 MoE sorted-A TMA on H200, 6.0–7.6% E2E throughput (#64760).
    • FP8 KV cache for DSpark and DFlash drafts (#63841, #64612, #65553).
    • FP32 indexer MQA logits restored for GLM-5/GLM-5.3/HY-V4, with new --attention-config.indexer_logits_dtype (#64580).
    • Fused KDA convs fix stale weights after RL refit (#60991).
  • Muse Spark
    • Opt-in Muse Spark Open specialized decode on GB300 (#64077).
    • One RoPE cache shared across layers: 11.5 GiB per GPU saved, 14.5% more KV cache on 8×B200 (#65206).
    • GEMM and communication+norm fusions (#65438, #64638); hybrid DeepGEMM MegaMoE / TRT-LLM for NVFP4 (#64525).
    • CUDA routing kernel (#64553), MegaMoE JIT warmup (#63920), DSpark draft loading fix (#65125).
  • MiniMax-M3 / M3.1
    • Sequence parallelism and GEMM-RS for TP + MegaMoE, 14–20% lower P50 TTFT (#64659), also with PP (#65537).
    • Fused norm + MXFP8 quant, 1.39–1.60× (#64852).
    • Triton query-tiled sparse prefill on Hopper (#57420); SM90 split-K indexer (#64037).
    • No host sync in prefill metadata (#65883); NVFP4 MegaMoE warmup (#66227); fmha_sm100 indexer updates (#66228).
    • Fixes: M3.1 prefill workspace (#64856), sequence parallelism (#65496), encoder CUDA graphs (#65226).
  • Kimi
    • Opt-in --attention-backend KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA for agentic workloads on Blackwell (#63638).
    • Kimi-K3 MegaMoE symmetric buffer 10.73 → 2.50 GiB per GPU at TP8 EP (#63541).
    • FlashInfer fused FP8 chunked-context K/V pack (#61527).
    • Fixes: KDA prefill OOM (#63989), NaNs via FlashKDA/FlashMLA pins (#64759), sleep mode (#64583, #66273).
    • Kimi K3.1 groundwork landed (#66030, #66028), but K3.1 is not servable in this release.
  • Qwen
    • Qwen3.5: breakable CUDA graphs instead of torch.compile (#51012); fused norm/gate + quant (#64509) and AR + norm + quant (#64723); GDN in_proj overlap (#64425, #64999).
    • GDN prefill state gather/scatter fused for Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5 and Kimi KDA, 1.16–1.50× (#66064).
    • Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: PLE disk offload via --engram-config '{"disk_offload": true}' (27 GiB less on DGX Spark, #59958), PP (#60234), shared QSA top-k buffer (#65619), loading fixes (#62318, #65812, #64820, #60490).
    • Fixes: long-context int32 overflow (#63761), multi-layer MTP (#62111).
  • Other models
    • Step5 MegaMoE with PP (#65504) and KV block sizing (#65153).
    • Gemma 4: multimodal encoder DP (#60314), PP (#65989), FA4 FP8 MMA on SM90 (#60372).
    • Moved to the Transformers modeling backend: OLMoE (#63384), Gemma v1 and StableLM (#66393), Aria (#59767; temporarily about 11% less KV cache and 25% lower image throughput).
    • Matryoshka dimensions for EmbeddingGemma 2 (#64885, #60978); RADIO C-RADIO v2/v3/v4 (#58468).
    • Qwen3-ASR on the upstream Transformers config; no --hf-overrides needed for the ForceAligner (#66097, #63274).
    • Fixes: GPT-OSS MXFP4 LoRA (#65825), PLaMo3 GPTQ (#62836), Ling3 (#65088), DomynEdge (#66819).
  • Multimodal
    • Encoder CUDA graphs for Pixtral/Mistral3 (#56277), shared capture buffers (#65084), one replay per batch up to encoder_cudagraph_max_token_budget (#65227).
    • On-device input normalization for Nemotron VL (#57924), Gemma 3 (#64487), Gemma 4 (#65577).
    • --mm-encoder-tp-mode data for MiMo-V2.6 (#64179).
    • Fixes: FlashInfer ViT attention on GLM-4.1V/GLM-OCR/GLM-5.3-Flash (#65778), Qwen3-Omni and Qwen2.5-Omni video budgets (#66017, #66190), dots_ocr with TP (#64543), embedding-only startup (#65689), media cache eviction (#65363).
Engine core
  • Extensible KV cache
    • On by default on CUDA and ROCm (#56492).
    • Headroom for measured allocator fragmentation, validated on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 at TP8+EP on 8×H200 (#67296).
    • Fixes: sizing and startup OOMs (#67485, #66523, #66731, #66197, #65554), connectors that failed to start (#65225), up to 84% undersized caches on DGX Spark (#65413), --max-model-len auto (#65463).

  • Model Runner V2
    • The only runner after MRV1's removal (#63373); DBO with spec decode and DCP (#61464).
    • Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes (#63406).
    • Staged writes copied straight into UVA (#63633); idle sampler writes skipped, about 10–11% faster small-batch decode (#62748).
    • Sampler warmed up after graph capture to stop memory growth under load (#62560).
    • Lower peak memory for chunked prompt logprobs (#64841, #64914); Triton ReplaySSM (#65033).
    • NVIDIA Confidential Computing decode fixes (#59981).
  • Speculative decoding
